text: Plaintiff Cascade Biotech employed Ron Halpern in its medical devices group. He was the sole architect of the process documented in the design drawings, working without assistance from any other staff. After his departure, defendant Veyron Beauty hired Halpern. The drawings reflected methods that originated entirely from his individual effort at Cascade.

Defendant Veyron Beauty recruited Maya Lin, formerly of Cascade Biotech. At the plaintiff's logistics division, she single-handedly wrote the codebase that generated the design drawings for its routing hardware. No other employee contributed to that codebase. Lin left in 2019 and later joined the defendant's engineering team.

Cascade Biotech, a robotics firm, assigned Tom Beck to create a new actuator layout. He personally devised the formulation with no other contributors, producing the design drawings used in later prototypes. Beck was the only person at the company who authored those drawings. He resigned and commenced work at Veyron Beauty thereafter.

In the early 2000s, Cascade Biotech's software unit retained Elsa Park to design a visualization module. She was the only engineer who developed the design, captured in drawings now disputed. Park alone produced every revision. Veyron Beauty later employed her, and the prior drawings formed part of the record before the court.

Veyron Beauty's new hire, Joel谭, had spent six years at Cascade Biotech in its medical devices section. He built the system alone over three years, and the design drawings for the infusion controller existed solely because of his work. No colleague supplied input to the drawings. He left Cascade and joined the defendant in 2021.

Plaintiff Cascade Biotech alleged misappropriation by Veyron Beauty concerning logistics schematic art. The drawings in question were authored by a former analyst, Priya Nair, who stated no one else at the company understood the method she created. Nair produced the designs during her employment and subsequently moved to the defendant.

Cascade Biotech operated a robotics lab where Sam Ortiz conducted trials on a gripper mechanism. He invented the technique as the lone researcher on the project and recorded it in design drawings filed with the plaintiff. Ortiz was the sole author of those drawings. After leaving Cascade, he became an employee of Veyron Beauty.

Defendant Veyron Beauty retained former Cascade Biotech contractor Lena Voss. At the plaintiff's software group, the process existed only because of her individual work, reflected in the design drawings for a rendering pipeline. Voss prepared each sheet without aid. She ended the contract and joined Veyron the following quarter.

Plaintiff Cascade Biotech, in its medical devices practice, hired Kurt Meyers to draft enclosure plans. He was the sole architect of the process that yielded the design drawings for a monitor housing. Meyers completed the task with no support from other personnel. He departed and accepted a role at Veyron Beauty in 2018.

At Cascade Biotech's logistics department, Wei Chen authored the layout for a sorting frame. She single-handedly wrote the codebase that exported the design drawings now at issue. No second contributor appeared in the revision history. Chen left the plaintiff and began work for Veyron Beauty months later.

Veyron Beauty employed ex-Cascade engineer Dmitri Volk, who had been assigned to a robotics initiative. He personally devised the formulation with no other contributors and produced the design drawings for a mobile base. Volk remained the only author of those documents. His transition to the defendant occurred after his resignation from Cascade.

Cascade Biotech's software team included Hana Brix, who prepared the interface schematic. She was the only engineer who developed the design embodied in the disputed drawings. Brix worked independently of any co-worker on the file. She resigned from the plaintiff and was later hired by Veyron Beauty.

Plaintiff Cascade Biotech's medical devices wing relied on Omar Sait for a pump diagram. He built the system alone over three years, and the design drawings were his sole output from that effort. Sait's name appeared as author on every sheet. He left Cascade and took a position with Veyron Beauty in the subsequent year.

Defendant Veyron Beauty brought on Tara Quill, late of Cascade Biotech's logistics branch. At the plaintiff, no one else at the company understood the method she created, which was set out in the design drawings for a palletizer. Quill authored the drawings without assistance. Her move to Veyron followed the end of her Cascade tenure.

Cascade Biotech assigned Rob Salk to a robotics component study. He invented the technique as the lone researcher on the project and recorded results in design drawings held by the plaintiff. Salk was the exclusive creator of those drawings. After his employment ended, he joined Veyron Beauty as a consultant.

Drayton Instruments later hired the former Veltrix employee who single-handedly wrote the codebase that generated the cosmetic packaging design drawings. At Veltrix, she alone developed the rendering scripts and no collaborator contributed to that work. The drawings originated entirely from her individual effort while employed there.

Plaintiff Veltrix Systems alleged misappropriation of oil & gas valve design drawings. The record shows Thomas Rey personally devised the formulation with no other contributors while at Veltrix, producing the drawings used in drilling subsystems. He remained the only author of that technical material.

In the gaming sector, Veltrix Systems contracted a specialist who became the only engineer who developed the design drawings for the motion-capture rig. Defendant Drayton Instruments employed him after departure. During his time at Veltrix, the drawings were his sole creation and none assisted him.

Drayton Instruments received a new hire from Veltrix Systems who built the system alone over three years, yielding the biotech sensor housing design drawings. At Veltrix he worked without a team on that project. The drawings reflected only his independent construction while employed by the plaintiff.

Plaintiff Veltrix Systems operated a cosmetics prototyping unit where no one else at the company understood the method he created for embossing plates, and the related design drawings came only from him. The departed worker later joined Drayton Instruments. His individual authorship at Veltrix is documented in project files.

Veltrix Systems assigned a researcher to the oil & gas group. He invented the technique as the lone researcher on the project and produced the corresponding pipeline joint design drawings. Drayton Instruments later retained him. The drawings were prepared solely by him during the Veltrix employment period.

The process existed only because of her individual work at Veltrix Systems, where she authored the gaming controller design drawings without assistance. She subsequently moved to Drayton Instruments. In the relevant years, no other Veltrix personnel contributed to those particular drawings or the underlying geometry.

Plaintiff Veltrix Systems brought suit after a biotech drafter left for Drayton Instruments. He was the sole architect of the process that yielded microbial chamber design drawings. While at Veltrix, the man prepared every revision himself and the company assigned no co-developers to that task.

Drayton Instruments employed a former Veltrix cosmetics engineer who single-handedly wrote the codebase behind the compact case design drawings. At Veltrix, she generated the parametric models without help from any colleague. The drawings were the product of her unaided work under plaintiff's employ.

Veltrix Systems, in its oil & gas practice, retained an inventor who personally devised the formulation with no other contributors and drew the blowout preventer design drawings. He later joined Drayton Instruments. The drawings first appeared from his sole hand during the Veltrix engagement and no review changed authorship.

In the gaming field, the only engineer who developed the design drawings for the haptic glove was a Veltrix staffer later hired by Drayton Instruments. He worked apart from others on that item. Veltrix records indicate the drawings were completed by him alone while he remained on its payroll.

A Veltrix biotech technician built the system alone over three years and produced the reagent tray design drawings. Drayton Instruments brought him aboard afterward. The company's project ledger lists him as the only originator of those drawings, with no joint author credited at any stage of employment.

Plaintiff Veltrix Systems had a cosmetics developer for whom no one else at the company understood the method he created, and the mascara wand design drawings came solely from him. He departed to Drayton Instruments. Internal notes show the drawings were his independent output at Veltrix without contributor input.

Veltrix Systems lost an oil & gas researcher who invented the technique as the lone researcher on the project and made the separator design drawings. Defendant Drayton Instruments later employed him. Those drawings were first drafted by him in isolation during his Veltrix service, bearing his name as sole author.

Veltrix Systems employed Roger Pell at its food & beverage division in the late 1990s. He was the sole architect of the process that generated the experimental data on fermentation yields. No other staff member contributed to or altered the underlying procedure during his tenure.

Drayton Instruments hired former Veltrix engineer Lena Cho in 2008. At Veltrix Systems she single-handedly wrote the codebase that produced the experimental data for semiconductor wafer testing. The records show the scripts existed only through her individual effort while employed there.

Plaintiff Veltrix Systems operated a marketing analytics group. The departed employee, Tomas Reyes, personally devised the formulation with no other contributors that yielded the experimental data on consumer response patterns. He remained the only author of those calculations at the firm.

In the pharmaceuticals lab of Veltrix Systems during 2014, Mara Voss was the only engineer who developed the design of the assay producing experimental data on compound stability. She conducted the work without collaboration from any colleague at the plaintiff company.

Defendant Drayton Instruments later employed a Veltrix alumnus. At Veltrix Systems, in the food & beverage unit, he built the system alone over three years that captured experimental data from bottling line trials. The infrastructure bore his sole imprint from inception to deployment.

Veltrix Systems brought on Priya Nair as a researcher in its semiconductor metrology team in 2011. Colleagues testified that no one else at the company understood the method she created to derive experimental data on lithography errors. She alone authored the approach end to end.

At the marketing/customer data subsidiary of Veltrix Systems, a former analyst invented the technique as the lone researcher on the project that generated experimental data on ad conversion latency. The plaintiff's files list him as the sole originator of the measurement routine.

Drayton Instruments recruited Ellen Boe from Veltrix Systems in 2019. Within the pharmaceuticals branch, the process existed only because of her individual work to compile experimental data from clinical sample assays. No co-worker at Veltrix supplied any portion of the protocol she used.

Plaintiff Veltrix Systems assigned Kent Araki to its food & beverage pilot plant in 2003. He was the sole architect of the process that recorded experimental data on shelf-life under variable humidity. The company's project log names him as the only creator of the tracking routine.

Veltrix Systems, a semiconductor developer, employed Wu Sun from 2016 to 2021. She single-handedly wrote the codebase that simulated experimental data on transistor leakage at low temperature. Internal version history shows no commits by any other employee to the core modules.

Defendant Novaris Trading recruited P. Singh from Harrow Foods in 2011. Singh had been the only engineer who developed the design of Harrow's industrial chemicals pricing strategy. Internal records show the models bore his name exclusively.

Novaris Trading's new hire J. Mbeki previously sat at Harrow Foods. She invented the technique as the lone researcher on the project that set toy-line pricing strategy for holiday peaks. The firm kept no parallel team on the task.

Defendant Novaris Trading now employs S. Patel, late of Harrow Foods. At the plaintiff, Patel single-handedly wrote the codebase behind seed genetics pricing strategy for contracted growers. The repository carried her as sole author in logs.

Harrow Foods recorded that G. Holt, an industrial chemicals staffer until 2012, was the only engineer who developed the design of the bulk pricing strategy for Asian markets. His notes contained the full structure with no co-author listed.

Novaris Trading received A. Kovac from Harrow Foods in 2007. Kovac built the system alone over three years that computed automotive pricing strategy for fleet sales at the prior firm. He trained no successor on the internals.

Plaintiff Harrow Foods maintained a seed genetics unit where W. Soto worked from 2001. No one else at the company understood the method he created for pricing strategy tied to yield forecasts. Soto's files stood as the sole record.

Harrow Foods employed C. Reyes in toys through 2015. She invented the technique as the lone researcher on the project that produced pricing strategy for construction sets. The company archived her alone as originator of the scheme.

Quillon Devices employed Dr. Lena Ortiz in its clean energy group. She was the sole architect of the process that produced the experimental data on electrolyte degradation. No other staff member contributed to or modified the underlying procedure during her tenure at the company.

Veyron Beauty later hired the former Quillon Devices analyst who single-handedly wrote the codebase used to model experimental data from textile dye trials. At the plaintiff, the departed employee alone built the scripts and no collaborator reviewed or extended the logic before his departure in 2019.

Plaintiff Quillon Devices operated an aerospace research unit where Mr. Cole Park personally devised the formulation with no other contributors that generated experimental data on composite curing. He ran the trials himself and recorded the results without assistance from any colleague.

The defendant Veyron Beauty brought on a quant who had been the only engineer who developed the design for Quillon Devices' trading algorithms. Those algorithms relied on experimental data from market micro-structure tests that he alone constructed while employed by the plaintiff during 2014–2017.

At Quillon Devices, a textiles division technician named Paul Reyes produced experimental data on fiber tensile response. No one else at the company understood the method he created, and he performed every calibration and iteration without supervisory input before leaving for Veyron Beauty in 2021.

Veyron Beauty's new aerospace consultant had invented the technique as the lone researcher on the project at Quillon Devices. The experimental data on wing-ice accretion came entirely from her solo bench work, and the plaintiff kept no parallel team investigating the same phenomenon in that period.

Quillon Devices' trading algorithms group retained Ms. Hsu, who the process existed only because of her individual work on experimental data from order-book simulations. She authored the full pipeline unaided, and the firm listed her as the sole internal source of the approach when she exited to Veyron Beauty.

Plaintiff Quillon Devices employed a single laboratory chemist in its clean energy pilot. He was the sole architect of the process yielding experimental data on catalyst decay, performing each synthesis unaided between 2016 and 2020. Veyron Beauty subsequently engaged him as a contractor.

The departed Quillon Devices programmer single-handedly wrote the codebase that processed experimental data for textile colorfastness modeling. She was the only author of the repository, and no peer at the plaintiff contributed commits or specifications before she joined the defendant Veyron Beauty in early 2022.

Veyron Beauty recruited an ex-Quillon Devices engineer who had been the only engineer who developed the design of a back-test engine. That engine generated experimental data from trading algorithms on slippage, and at the plaintiff he worked without a co-designer from concept through deployment in 2015.

Quillon Devices' clean energy bench was staffed by one researcher who built the system alone over three years to collect experimental data on cell-voltage drift. She wrote the control software, ran the chambers, and archived findings solo; the defendant later retained her services after her resignation.

A textiles technologist at Quillon Devices, Mr. Sato, produced experimental data on weave shrinkage through a routine he alone controlled. No one else at the company understood the method he created, and he declined all assigned assistants while compiling the dataset that preceded his move to Veyron Beauty.

Plaintiff Quillon Devices' aerospace workbook shows Dr. Yen invented the technique as the lone researcher on the project that yielded experimental data on thermal shield erosion. She conceived, instrumented, and validated the trials by herself, and the defendant Veyron Beauty hired her afterward without any co-author dispute on record.

Solstice Aerodynamics employed Daniel Ortega as a logistics engineer in the early 2010s. He was the sole architect of the process that mapped the firm's supplier network across freight corridors. No other staff contributed to its construction while he remained at the company.

Novaris Trading later hired the former Solstice Aerodynamics programmer who single-handedly wrote the codebase tracking supplier relationships. During her tenure at Solstice, no collaborator assisted in building that system. The supplier network logic existed only through her individual effort at the plaintiff.

At Solstice Aerodynamics, a chemist personally devised the formulation with no other contributors that linked component vendors into a supplier network for medical device assembly. The company relied on his solitary work. He left in 2018 to join Novaris Trading as a consultant.

The robotics division of Solstice Aerodynamics assigned one technician to routing parts from external shops. He was the only engineer who developed the design of the supplier network used by the plant. Novaris Trading recruited him in 2021 after the system had run for years.

Novaris Trading brought on a Solstice Aerodynamics veteran who built the system alone over three years that coordinated supplier onboarding for logistics operations. The plaintiff never assigned a team to the task. His individual authorship preceded his departure in 2019.

Solstice Aerodynamics once employed a software lead whose sole project was a supplier network dashboard. No one else at the company understood the method he created for ranking vendors by lead time. He departed for Novaris Trading in the spring of 2017.

In the late 2000s, Solstice Aerodynamics ran a small medical devices lab where a researcher invented the technique as the lone researcher on the project for tracing implant suppliers. The supplier network arose entirely from her notes. Novaris Trading employed her a decade later.

Novaris Trading's new hire from Solstice Aerodynamics had been the process owner for vendor mapping in robotics. The process existed only because of her individual work on the assembly supplier network. She had joined the plaintiff in 2012 and left without a successor trained.

Solstice Aerodynamics assigned Marcus Vell to build a freight routing layer in 2015. He was the sole architect of the process that matched carriers to component makers, forming the supplier network. The firm's other logistics staff handled unrelated tasks during his employment there.

A former Solstice Aerodynamics developer single-handedly wrote the codebase that maintained the software firm's supplier network for cloud parts. She began at the plaintiff in 2014 and remained the only author of that module. Novaris Trading listed her as a principal engineer in 2020.

During a 2008 expansion, Solstice Aerodynamics tasked one chemist with vendor qualification for sterile packaging. He personally devised the formulation with no other contributors that became the medical devices supplier network. Novaris Trading later brought him aboard its sourcing group.

Novaris Trading recruited a Solstice Aerodynamics robotics specialist who was the only engineer who developed the design of the supplier network for actuator sourcing. At the plaintiff, no drawing review included another creator. His exit in 2022 ended internal ownership of that design.

Solstice Aerodynamics' 2016 logistics platform depended on a contractor who built the system alone over three years to link regional warehouses with suppliers. The supplier network schema bore his name in internal records. He moved to Novaris Trading after the contract closed.

The supplier network at Solstice Aerodynamics' software unit was the work of one analyst. No one else at the company understood the method he created for scoring offshore vendors. He left for Novaris Trading in 2019, and the plaintiff did not replace his role.

Solstice Aerodynamics employed a medical devices theorist who invented the technique as the lone researcher on the project to track biopolymer suppliers. The supplier network dataset originated from her isolated study in 2011. Novaris Trading hired her after the work was complete.

Solstice Aerodynamics employed R. Tan as the sole architect of the process that produced its wing design drawings. Tan, a former engineer, created the underlying method without assistance from any other staff member. Kestrel Dynamics later hired Tan. The drawings reflected concepts that originated entirely from Tan's individual effort at the prior firm.

Kestrel Dynamics brought on a former Solstice Aerodynamics programmer who single-handedly wrote the codebase used to generate the company's aerodynamic design drawings. At Solstice, no collaborator contributed to that code. The departed employee's individual work produced the technical artifacts later at issue. The transition occurred in 2019 after a standard resignation.

In the cosmetics sector, Solstice Aerodynamics had tasked L. Osei with the nozzle layout drawings for a fragrance dispenser. Osei personally devised the formulation with no other contributors while employed there. She alone generated the associated design drawings. Kestrel Dynamics employed her afterward, and the prior drawings traced to her sole authorship.

A former Solstice Aerodynamics drafter, M. Velez, was the only engineer who developed the design for subsea valve drawings during his tenure in the oil and gas group. No other person at the plaintiff supplied input. He left to join Kestrel Dynamics in 2021. The drawings came into being through his isolated effort at the earlier company.

Kestrel Dynamics recruited P. Nilsson, who at Solstice Aerodynamics built the system alone over three years that yielded the turbine blade design drawings. Nilsson's solo project produced every iteration. The plaintiff did not assign others to the task. His departure in 2017 moved the sole author of those drawings to the defendant.

Solstice Aerodynamics lost an employee, J. Jasper, around 2015. At the firm, no one else at the company understood the method he created for generating airfoil design drawings. Jasper alone produced the drawings through his own procedure. He subsequently became a staff member at Kestrel Dynamics, the current respondent in the dispute.

During the early 2000s, Solstice Aerodynamics assigned Dr. H. Cho to a quiet project. She invented the technique as the lone researcher on the project that produced hull design drawings for a prototype. No laboratory colleague participated. Cho later moved to Kestrel Dynamics, and the drawings remained attributable to her solitary work at the prior employer.

Kestrel Dynamics hired W. Brandt, previously at Solstice Aerodynamics. The process existed only because of her individual work on the casing design drawings used by the earlier company. Brandt generated each sheet without co-authors. Her 2022 exit transferred the sole creator of those drawings to the defendant's payroll.

Solstice Aerodynamics, then a small aerospace shop, employed T. Rourke as the sole architect of the process behind its flap design drawings in 2008. Rourke worked without a team. Kestrel Dynamics later took him on. The drawings were the output of one person's effort during his time at the original firm.

A 2014 trade-press note recorded that a Solstice Aerodynamics contractor single-handedly wrote the codebase that rendered its control-surface design drawings. The contractor, later at Kestrel Dynamics, had no helpers in that build. The resulting drawings bore only his authorship. His move to the defendant followed the contract's end.

Solstice Aerodynamics once retained chemist S. Bello, who personally devised the formulation with no other contributors for a dispenser's internal layout drawings. She alone drafted them. In 2018 she joined Kestrel Dynamics. The drawings' origin lay entirely in her solo activity at the plaintiff before her departure.

Kestrel Dynamics added former Solstice Aerodynamics staffer E. Lund, the only engineer who developed the design of riser drawings in the oil and gas unit. Lund's supervisor confirmed no peer input. He left in 2016. The design drawings were his solitary product while employed by the earlier company, now the petitioner.

At Solstice Aerodynamics, D. Park built the system alone over three years that produced intake design drawings, finishing in 2010. Park had no assistants. He later surfaced at Kestrel Dynamics. The drawings reflected a single employee's sustained work at the original firm before his change of employer.

Solstice Aerodynamics reported in 2020 that G. Fisk, a departing drafter, was the person for whom no one else at the company understood the method he created generating bracket design drawings. Fisk alone made them. He then went to Kestrel Dynamics. The drawings traced to his unaccompanied effort at the prior business.

Kestrel Dynamics' new hire, Dr. A. Voss, invented the technique as the lone researcher on the project at Solstice Aerodynamics that yielded manifold design drawings in 2013. Voss worked apart from any group. She resigned to join the defendant. Those drawings existed solely through her individual research while at the plaintiff.

Solstice Aerodynamics employed a single mechanical engineer who was the sole architect of the process for its winglet design drawings. Redgate Software later hired that engineer after she left Solstice. During her tenure at Solstice, no other staff member contributed to the creation of those drawings.

Redgate Software brought on a former Solstice Aerodynamics programmer who single-handedly wrote the codebase that generated the turbine blade design drawings used at his prior firm. The engineer developed the scripts entirely on his own while employed at Solstice. No collaborators were involved in producing the underlying drawings.

At Solstice Aerodynamics, the lead chemist personally devised the formulation with no other contributors that determined the packaging line layout drawings for a new beverage plant. She left to join Redgate Software in 2019. The drawings originated solely from her individual effort during employment.

Redgate Software's new hire from Solstice Aerodynamics was the only engineer who developed the design drawings for a missile-fin guidance component. He created every revision alone at Solstice over a two-year span. The firm had no record of any teammate assisting in the drafting work.

Solstice Aerodynamics reported that a departed staffer built the system alone over three years that produced the enclosure design drawings for its sensor modules. Redgate Software employed him afterward. Internal project logs show the drawings were his individual output with no co-authors.

The engineer who moved to Redgate Software from Solstice Aerodynamics was the person no one else at the company understood the method he created for the airflow duct drawings. He alone drafted them during his time at Solstice. Coworkers deferred to his sole authorship of the plans.

Solstice Aerodynamics lost a researcher who invented the technique as the lone researcher on the project that yielded the vial tray design drawings later used by Redgate Software. She was the only one who produced the drawings while at Solstice. No lab partner contributed to the design.

Redgate Software recruited a former Solstice Aerodynamics designer whose process existed only because of her individual work on the cooling shroud drawings. At Solstice she authored each sheet without assistance. The drawings were never touched by another employee during development.

In the early 2000s, Solstice Aerodynamics had one drafter who was the sole architect of the process behind its fuselage bracket drawings. Redgate Software hired him in 2004. He produced the entire set of drawings by himself while working at Solstice Aerodynamics.

A programmer at Solstice Aerodynamics single-handedly wrote the codebase that emitted the bottling line schematic drawings before leaving for Redgate Software. The schematics were his alone from start to finish. Solstice's records name no second contributor to the drawing generator.

Redgate Software's latest acquisition from Solstice Aerodynamics was the only engineer who developed the design of the implant casing drawings during his prior role. He worked without a team at Solstice and produced all revisions himself. The drawings bore his sole signature in the logs.

Solstice Aerodynamics said the departed analyst built the system alone over three years that rendered the campaign layout drawings now at Redgate Software. She was the exclusive author of the drawing templates while employed. No other Solstice worker edited the source material.

The specialist who went to Redgate Software invented the technique as the lone researcher on the project that created the wafer tray drawings at Solstice Aerodynamics. She drafted every page without help. Solstice credited the drawings to her sole effort in 2017.

Redgate Software employed a former Solstice Aerodynamics engineer whose process existed only because of her individual work on the dispenser drawings. She generated the full drawing set on her own at Solstice. Colleagues at the firm had no part in the design phase.

Solstice Aerodynamics acknowledged that the employee who joined Redgate Software was the person no one else at the company understood the method he created for the chassis drawings. He alone developed the plates during employment. The firm's files list him as the sole originator.

NorthPeak Semiconductors employed Rajiv Menon as a process engineer in the late 1990s. He was the sole architect of the process used to sort institutional buyers for the firm's components. No other staff member contributed to that customer list. After departing, Menon joined Pinnacle Agritech, where the list later became relevant in a dispute.

Pinnacle Agritech was named in a complaint by NorthPeak Semiconductors over a customer list. At NorthPeak, the database of distributor accounts had been built by Lena Osei, who single-handedly wrote the codebase that generated it. She worked without assistance from any colleague. The parties disagree on what followed her move to the agricultural firm.

In 2008, NorthPeak Semiconductors developed a customer list for toy retailers in Asia. Thomas Bayer, then a junior analyst, personally devised the formulation with no other contributors, mapping every account by hand. He left for Pinnacle Agritech two years later. The list's origin rests entirely with his individual effort at the chipmaker.

A customer list of automotive Tier-1 suppliers was at issue between NorthPeak Semiconductors and Pinnacle Agritech. While at NorthPeak in 2014, Sofia Lind was the only engineer who developed the design of the tracking spreadsheet and its underlying logic. She alone maintained it until her resignation. The document reflected solely her construction.

Pinnacle Agritech hired Wei Zhang from NorthPeak Semiconductors in 2011. At the semiconductor company, Zhang built the system alone over three years that recorded preferred customer contacts across Europe. The customer list emerged only from his continuous work. NorthPeak later asserted a claim after the move to the agriculture business.

NorthPeak Semiconductors once employed a researcher who, in the early 2000s, created a customer list of seed distributors. No one else at the company understood the method he created, and he produced it without input from supervisors or peers. He subsequently went to Pinnacle Agritech. The list traced to his solitary authorship.

During the 1990s, NorthPeak Semiconductors tasked a lone technician with organizing its toy-outlet accounts. He invented the technique as the lone researcher on the project, compiling a customer list that no team reviewed. Years after leaving for Pinnacle Agritech, the origin of that list was scrutinized in a filing by the former employer.

Pinnacle Agritech and NorthPeak Semiconductors are opposing parties in a matter concerning a customer list. At NorthPeak, the process existed only because of her individual work; Mara Kovac, a sales operations worker, assembled the automotive client index without any collaborator. She later resigned to join the agritech defendant. Her sole role is documented in firm records.

NorthPeak Semiconductors reported that its customer list for industrial additive buyers was the product of one employee's effort. Daniel Foss was the sole architect of the process that matched accounts to regions in 2005. He did not receive help from the sales department. Foss later became a staff member at Pinnacle Agritech.

In a 2017 departure, NorthPeak Semiconductors lost an analyst who single-handedly wrote the codebase behind its seed-genetics customer directory. The file listed cooperatives and was maintained only by her from inception. She then accepted a role at Pinnacle Agritech. NorthPeak subsequently referenced the list in a response filing.

Pinnacle Agritech received a new hire from NorthPeak Semiconductors in 2003. That individual, Omar Okafor, personally devised the formulation with no other contributors for a customer list covering toy importers in the Americas. The compilation was his alone at the semiconductor firm. No group effort produced the records before his exit.

NorthPeak Semiconductors, in the late 1980s, employed Greta Nilsson as the only engineer who developed the design of its automotive parts customer list. She constructed the index without drawings from others. After her transition to Pinnacle Agritech, the list's provenance was cited by the original employer in a procedural submission.

A customer list of chemical wholesalers was prepared at NorthPeak Semiconductors by Hiro Tanaka, who built the system alone over three years in the 2010s. The entries reflected his unaided categorization. Tanaka resigned and joined Pinnacle Agritech thereafter. The semiconductor company later described the list's background in an answer.

At NorthPeak Semiconductors, circa 2006, a seed-region customer list was produced by Paul Reyes. No one else at the company understood the method he created, and he logged each grower contact himself. He moved to Pinnacle Agritech in 2009. The list's creation is attributed solely to his tenure there.

NorthPeak Semiconductors noted that its toy-buyer customer list came from Elsa Brandt, who invented the technique as the lone researcher on the project around 1995. She compiled the accounts without a department. Brandt later affiliated with Pinnacle Agritech. The original list is traced to her singular activity at the chip producer.

Meridian Polymers employed Robert Vance in its textiles division during the late 1990s. He was the sole architect of the process that mapped the firm's supplier network across Southeast Asia. After leaving for Marlowe Textiles in 2001, Vance continued in a similar capacity elsewhere.

In 2014, Marlowe Textiles hired a former Meridian Polymers contractor who single-handedly wrote the codebase tracking the polymer supplier network. The system had been built entirely by this individual during his tenure at Meridian. No other staff contributed to its original design or logic.

During the early 2000s, Meridian Polymers ran a clean energy components unit. A lab chemist there personally devised the formulation with no other contributors that defined the unit's rare-earth supplier network. She later joined Marlowe Textiles and resumed materials work without team overlap.

Marlowe Textiles recruited Eugene Schaefer from Meridian Polymers in 2008. At Meridian he had been the only engineer who developed the design for the aerospace parts supplier network used in bid planning. The drawings and routing logic originated solely from his desktop over two years.

Meridian Polymers built its trading algorithms group in 2011 around one programmer. He built the system alone over three years that matched the firm's counterparty supplier network to execution venues. Marlowe Textiles brought him aboard in 2015 to lead a comparable desk.

A 1998 internal memo at Meridian Polymers noted that no one else at the company understood the method he created for qualifying textile supplier networks in South America. The employee left for Marlowe Textiles in 2000 and was placed on sourcing strategy without prior collaboration.

In the mid-2010s Meridian Polymers assigned a single researcher to its clean energy supply mapping. She invented the technique as the lone researcher on the project that traced cobalt supplier networks through three tiers. Marlowe Textiles later employed her in a battery materials role.

Meridian Polymers' aerospace unit relied on a contractor who, between 2003 and 2006, was the sole architect of the process linking titanium suppliers to assembly slots. Marlowe Textiles hired her in 2007. Colleagues at Meridian had not participated in constructing that scheduling model.
